title: A prisoner sings the churches' praises
sum: Ignatius, a prisoner from Antioch on his way to Rome, greets 'the church that is in Magnesia on the Maeander' (1:0). He has heard how well ordered their love for God is and writes gladly (1:1). In his chains he sings the praises of the churches and prays for three kinds of union: of Christ's flesh and spirit, of faith and love, and of Jesus and the Father. Whoever endures the abuse of 'the ruler of this age' will 'reach God' (1:2).
The words of 1:2 announce the letter: union with the overseer (2-7), the true Christ against those who deny his flesh and live 'by Judaism' (8-11), and prayer (14).

views.H: The setting is given at the end: Ignatius writes from Smyrna, with Ephesians and with Polycarp beside him (15:1). Eusebius names this letter second among the four from Smyrna (Church History 3.36.5).
views.N: 'The ruler of this age' takes up Paul's phrase in 1 Corinthians 2:6-8; 'reach God' is Ignatius's own, close to Paul's 'to leave and be with Christ' (Philippians 1:23).

settings.what: The greeting and why Ignatius writes
settings.to: The church at Magnesia on the Maeander, a city near Ephesus in the Roman province of Asia
settings.when: Under guard at Smyrna, on the way to Rome, after the Magnesians had sent their overseer, two elders and a deacon to him (2:1; 15:1)
settings.why: To thank the church for its delegates and to open what he wants for it: union in Christ's flesh and spirit and with its leaders. Lake: the immediate purpose of each letter but Romans 'is to thank the recipients for the kindness which they had shown to Ignatius'.
settings.readers: The Magnesian Christians who heard it read, among them their overseer Damas and the others who had met Ignatius (2:1); Lightfoot thinks the church went back to Paul's years in nearby Ephesus.

title: Damas, Bassus, Apollonius and Zotion
sum: Ignatius has seen the whole church in its four delegates: Damas the overseer, the elders Bassus and Apollonius, and the deacon Zotion, his 'fellow slave', who is subject to the overseer 'as to the grace of God' and to the elders 'as to the law of Jesus Christ' (2:1).
The Greek sentence is never finished (Lake's footnote); Lightfoot hears its main verb only in 6:1, 'I urge you'.

views.H: Lightfoot: the delegation 'comprised all orders of the ministry', which is why Ignatius can say he has seen the whole congregation in them (6:1).
views.C: One overseer, a council of elders and deacons appear here in one small church; on whether the New Testament knows such an order, see the cards at Acts 20:28 and Philippians 1:1.

settings.to: The Magnesian church, through its four delegates
settings.when: At Smyrna, as Ignatius looks back on their visit
settings.why: To honor the delegates by name, and to hold up Zotion's submission as the pattern the letter goes on to ask of all.
settings.readers: Damas, Bassus, Apollonius and Zotion heard themselves named before their own church when the letter was read; nothing else is known of them.

title: A young overseer
sum: The Magnesians' overseer is young. They are not to take advantage of that, but to give him all respect, as the elders already do: they defer not to him but 'to the Father of Jesus Christ, the overseer of all' (3:1). Hypocrisy toward the overseer who can be seen is an attempt to cheat the one who cannot be seen, and the reckoning is with God, 'who knows the hidden things' (3:2).

views.N: Paul tells the young Timothy, 'Let no one treat your youth with contempt' (1 Timothy 4:12). 1 Peter 2:25 calls Christ 'the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls'.
views.C: Ignatius grounds respect for the overseer in God the Father. Catholic teaching takes up the picture (Catechism 1549, citing 6:1); others read it as Ignatius's way of urging unity (see the note at 6:1).

settings.what: On respect for the young overseer
settings.to: The Magnesian church as a whole, and in it any who made light of Damas for his youth
settings.when: With Damas's visit fresh in mind
settings.why: To head off a problem a young leader faced: that people would humor him in public and ignore him in fact. Ignatius moves the matter from the man to God.
settings.readers: The congregation heard it in front of Damas himself, and the elders heard themselves praised for deferring to a younger man.

title: Christians in name only
sum: It is not enough to be called Christians; one must be Christians. Some 'call him overseer, yet they do everything without him'. Their meetings 'are not valid or held as commanded' (4:1).

views.H: The verse shows that some people, whom Ignatius does not name or place, used the overseer's title but acted without him. Ignatius uses the word 'valid' (bebaiōs) again of the thanksgiving in Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 8:1.
views.C: Who may lead the church's worship is the card at Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 8; the question of 'valid' meetings is the one that card answers for each church.

echoes: Acts 11:26; 1 Peter 4:16; Luke 6:46; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 8:1

settings.what: Against meetings apart from the overseer
settings.to: The Magnesians, warned about people who use the overseer's title but not his leadership
settings.why: To show that the name 'Christian' must be matched by a life lived with the church's leaders, and to name what he fears: separate gatherings.
settings.readers: The Magnesians, warned about people who, as Ignatius describes them, acknowledged the overseer in words only; he does not name them or say where they were.

title: Two coins
sum: Everything ends; death and life lie before us, and each goes 'to his own place' (5:1). Like two coins, each person bears a stamp: the unbelievers the world's, the believers 'the stamp of God the Father through Jesus Christ'. Unless we freely choose to die into Christ's suffering, his life is not in us (5:2).

views.N: 'His own place' is from Acts 1:25; the coin, Lake suggests, from Matthew 22:19-20. Paul's 'share his sufferings' (Philippians 3:10) and 'a death like his' (Romans 6:5) are close.
views.H: The call to choose death freely was not abstract for a prisoner in chains (1:2).

settings.what: The two ways and the two coins
settings.when: As the reason for the call to unity that follows in 6:1
settings.why: To set every choice in the church against the two ends, death and life, and to ask the hearers which stamp they bear.
settings.readers: Christians who used coins with the emperor's image every day would have heard the picture at once.

title: In the place of God
sum: Ignatius has seen the whole church in its delegates and loves it. So he urges: do everything in God's harmony, with 'the overseer presiding in the place of God, and the elders in the place of the council of the apostles', and the deacons 'entrusted with the ministry of Jesus Christ', who 'was with the Father before the ages and appeared at the end' (6:1). Let them respect one another, love one another in Christ, let nothing divide them, and be united with the overseer and those who preside, 'as a type and a lesson of incorruption' (6:2).
This is one of the lines most quoted in debates about bishops. Two witnesses read 'as a type of God' for 'in the place of God' (see the variant).
readings: Catholic teaching takes up Ignatius's picture of the three offices for the bishop as 'like the living image of God the Father' (Catechism 1549, citing this verse and Ignatius to the Trallians 3:1).
Read as a plea for unity

Ignatius uses the strongest pictures he has to hold a small church together. Lightfoot granted that the letters' language for the overseer is the strongest in Christian literature, but explained it by 'the needs and distractions of the age' (The Christian Ministry, pages 85-88).

views.H: Ignatius knows one overseer, a council of elders and deacons in Magnesia. Whether every church of his day had one overseer is another question: Polycarp's letter to Philippi names only 'elders and deacons' there (Polycarp to the Philippians 5:3).
views.N: In the New Testament the same leaders seem to be called 'elders' and 'overseers' (Acts 20:17, 28; Titus 1:5-7), and Philippi has several overseers (Philippians 1:1). Paul's 'we know no one by the flesh' (2 Corinthians 5:16) stands behind 6:2.
views.C: See the views note at 6:1 and the cards at Acts 20:28, Philippians 1:1, 1 Timothy 3 (bishops and elders) and 2 Timothy 2 (succession).

deep.b:
The Greek manuscript, the Latin and the long recension read eis topon theou, 'in the place of God'; the Syriac and the Armenian eis typon, 'as a type of God'. Lake prints 'place': Lightfoot 'prefers τύπον, but it seems to be more probably a softening of the rather startling τόπον by the Syriac translator.' Lightfoot's own case rests on the Syriac word, on Ignatius to the Trallians 3:1 ('the overseer is a type of the Father'), and on the Apostolic Constitutions, which repeat eis typon in a passage he calls 'obviously moulded after Ignatius'.

Either way the overseer stands for God and the elders for the apostles' council. 'Place' says he holds God's seat in the meeting; 'type' says he is a picture of God to it. The Catechism (1549) gives the 'type' wording of To the Trallians.

The overseer for God, the elders for the apostles, the deacons for the service of Jesus Christ: the same pattern returns in Ignatius to the Trallians 3:1, with the deacons 'as Jesus Christ'. Lightfoot summed it up: 'If the bishop occupies the place of God or of Jesus Christ, the presbyters are as the Apostles, as the council of God'. Ignatius does not say how the overseer was chosen, or that he succeeds the apostles; the apostles stand for the elders, not the overseer.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the seating plan of a meeting
deep.b: 'Preside' (prokathēmai) means 'sit in front'. Ignatius's words may picture the room where the church met: the overseer in the chair, the elders seated beside him like a council, the deacons moving among the people to serve. On that reading 'in the place of God' is, first of all, a seat, and 'type' a later explanation of what the seat means. This is my suggestion from the verb and from 13:1, 'that well-woven spiritual crown' of elders; Lightfoot notes the same verb for the bishop in later writers.

echoes: Acts 20:17; Acts 20:28; Titus 1:5-7; Philippians 1:1; 2 Corinthians 5:16; John 1:1; Ignatius to the Trallians 3:1

settings.what: The call to do everything with the overseer, elders and deacons
settings.to: The Magnesian church as a whole
settings.when: Taking up again the sentence broken off at 2:1
settings.why: To make the leaders of the church the visible center of its unity, so that no separate meeting (4:1) and no strange teaching (8:1) can split it.
settings.readers: Readers whose own overseer was young (3:1) heard him set 'in the place of God'; Lightfoot notes that the passage was later echoed in a church order, the Apostolic Constitutions.

title: One temple, one altar
sum: As the Lord did nothing without the Father, so the Magnesians must do nothing without the overseer and the elders. Nothing done on one's own will seem right; when they meet in one place, let there be 'one prayer, one request, one mind, one hope', in Jesus Christ (7:1). 'Run together as into one temple of God, as to one altar, to one Jesus Christ', who came from the one Father and went back to him (7:2).

views.N: Lake's margin gives John 5:19, 5:30 and 8:28 for the Son who does nothing on his own; 7:2 follows John 16:28. The string of 'one' recalls Ephesians 4:4-6.
views.C: 'One altar' with 'one overseer' becomes explicit in To the Philadelphians 4:1. Whether the Supper is a sacrifice is the card at Hebrews 10; Christ's presence in it, the card at Matthew 26:26.

echoes: John 5:19; John 5:30; John 8:28; John 16:28; Ephesians 4:4-6; Hebrews 13:10; Acts 2:1

settings.why: To picture unity as one building with one altar, so that a separate meeting looks like a second temple.
settings.readers: Readers in a city whose great temple of Artemis (Lightfoot) was its pride heard the church called 'one temple of God'.

title: The prophets lived by Christ
sum: Do not be led astray by 'other opinions' or 'old myths'. 'If we are still living by Judaism to this day, we admit that we have not received grace' (8:1). The prophets themselves 'lived by Christ Jesus' and were persecuted for it, inspired to convince the disobedient that there is one God, who made himself known through his Son, 'his Word, who came forth from silence' (8:2).
readings: Ignatius sets 'Judaism' and grace against each other: to keep living by the old ways is to deny that grace has come. Lightfoot reads 10:3 as a comparison of the two faiths: Christianity was 'a larger and better dispensation than Judaism'. The later history of Christian texts used against Jews is on the topic Christian Anti-Judaism and the Bible.

The same verses put the prophets on Christ's side: they 'lived by Christ Jesus'. The quarrel is not with Israel's Scriptures, which Ignatius quotes as 'it is written' (12:1), but with Christians who, in his view, made the old practices the rule of life.

views.H: Lake: 'it is disputed whether he means that this was an evil found in docetic circles, or that it was a danger threatening the church from other directions.' Lightfoot: 'a Docetic Judaism'.
views.N: 'Judaism' is Paul's word in Galatians 1:13-14; 'myths' are warned against in 1 Timothy 1:4 and Titus 1:14; the prophets who bore witness to Christ are 1 Peter 1:10-11.

deep.h: 'His Word, who came forth from silence'
deep.b:
Lake prints the reading of the Armenian and of Severus: 'his Word, who came forth from silence'. The Greek manuscript and the Latin have 'his eternal Word, not coming forth from silence'. Lake, with 'recent editors', calls the longer reading 'a doctrinal emendation due to fear of Gnostic theories in which Σιγή and Θεός were the original pair from which Λόγος emanated': some Gnostic teachers spoke of Silence as a heavenly being paired with God.

Lightfoot reads Ignatius's phrase not as such a theory but as a picture of revelation: 'σιγὴ and λόγος are correlative terms', and since the context is the incarnation ('made himself known ... the one who sent him'), the Word's coming forth from silence is his coming into the world. He compares Ignatius to the Ephesians 19:1, 'three mysteries ... which were done in God's quiet', and Romans 16:25, 'the mystery kept in silence for long ages'. Ignatius had already said that the Son 'was with the Father before the ages' (6:1).

echoes: Galatians 1:13-14; 1 Timothy 1:4; Titus 1:14; 1 Peter 1:10-11; Matthew 5:12; John 1:1; John 8:29; Romans 16:25

settings.to: The Magnesian church, warned against teachers Ignatius does not name
settings.when: After the call to unity, as its reason: unity guards against strange teaching (Lightfoot)
settings.why: To keep the church from a teaching that, as Ignatius sees it, makes the old practices the rule of Christian life and denies the reality of Christ's death (9:1). He tells them that the prophets were on Christ's side.
settings.readers: Christians in a city of Asia whose own Scriptures were the prophets; Ignatius says he does not know that any of them hold the teaching (11:1).
views: Lightfoot: the same teachers who denied the reality of Christ's death kept Jewish practices: 'a Docetic Judaism'.
Lake: it is disputed whether the Judaizing tendency belonged to docetic circles or came 'from other directions'.
Fritz Guy (1964): 'Judaizing' here is 'an inner, spiritual attitude', legalism, more than a set of practices.

title: Living by the Lord's day
sum: Ignatius argues from a condition: 'If, then, those who lived in the old ways came to a new hope, no longer keeping the Sabbath but living by the Lord's [day], on which our life also rose through him and through his death, which some deny ...' (9:1), then 'how will we be able to live without him?' (9:2). Even the prophets were his disciples in the Spirit, and when he came, he 'raised them from the dead' (9:2).

No early line is quoted more often in the argument over Sunday and the Sabbath. Both its text and its subject are argued: the one Greek manuscript reads 'the Lord's life', and readers differ on who 'those who lived in the old ways' were.
readings: Jewish believers had left the Sabbath and kept 'the Lord's day', the day of the resurrection. The Catechism quotes it so (Catechism 2175); Lightfoot reads it the same way, with the day standing for all that the resurrection means.
Read as a contrast of two ways of life

If the subject is the prophets (8:2), as Fritz Guy argues, they cannot have stopped keeping the Sabbath or kept Sunday; 'keeping the Sabbath' then means a legalistic way of life, and 'the Lord's' (day or life) its opposite. Guy concludes that the line 'can not at the present time properly be introduced as evidence' for keeping the Lord's day, nor ruled out as an allusion to it.

views.H: The Greek has the adjective kyriakē, 'the Lord's', with no word for 'day'; the Medicean manuscript adds 'life'. Lake prints the shorter text; Lightfoot defends it at length (see the variant).
views.N: Revelation 1:10 has the full phrase, 'the Lord's day'; the first day of the week is the day of the resurrection (Matthew 28:1) and of a gathering to break bread (Acts 20:7). Colossians 2:16-17 and Romans 14:5 speak of days. Matthew 27:52-53 and 1 Peter 3:19 stand behind 9:2.
views.C: The Catechism quotes 9:1 for Sunday replacing the Sabbath's 'ceremonial observance' (2175). Each church's teaching is on the cards at Revelation 1:10, Exodus 20 and Colossians 2; the views note at 9:1 gives the readings of this verse.

deep.b:
Ei oun hoi en palaiois pragmasin anastraphentes eis kainotēta elpidos ēlthon, mēketi sabbatizontes, alla kata kyriakēn zōntes, en hē kai hē zōē hēmōn aneteilen di' autou kai tou thanatou autou. Word by word: 'If then those who lived in old practices came into newness of hope, no longer sabbatizing but living according to the Lord's, on which also our life rose through him and his death ...'. The sentence is the 'if' half of the question in 9:2, 'how will we be able to live without him?'. 'On which' (en hē) is feminine, and Lightfoot argues it needs a day; Guy answers that it could refer to 'life'.

The manuscripts: the Greek (G, eleventh century, Guy) reads kata kyriakēn zōēn zōntes; the Latin secundum dominicam viventes; the Armenian, in Latin, 'the Lord's day, holy and first'. Lake, Lightfoot and Zahn print the text without 'life'.

Lake's footnote takes 9:2 'more probably' as the belief 'that Jesus by the descent into Hades set free, and took into Paradise, the righteous dead', found 'in many documents of a later date', above all the Gospel of Nicodemus (the Acts of Pilate). Lightfoot calls the descent 'a prominent place in the belief of the early Church' and finds its roots in 1 Peter 3:19 and 4:6. Matthew 27:52 tells of saints raised at Jesus's death. See the topic The Descent into Hades.

echoes: Revelation 1:10; Colossians 2:16-17; Romans 14:5; Hebrews 4:9; Matthew 28:1; Acts 20:7; Matthew 27:52-53; 1 Peter 3:19; 1 Peter 1:10-11; Matthew 23:8

settings.what: The Lord's day and the prophets
settings.when: In the middle of the warning against 'Judaism' (8:1-10:3)
settings.why: To argue from the greater to the lesser: if even those who lived in the old ways (Jewish believers, or the prophets) came to the new hope in Christ, Christians cannot go back to the old ways and live without him.
settings.readers: The Magnesian Christians, warned against teachers of 'Judaism' (8:1); Ignatius does not say whether the hearers or the teachers were Jews by birth or Gentiles, and readers differ on who the subject of 9:1 is.
views: Lightfoot: 'those who were brought up in the practices of Judaism'.
Fritz Guy reads the subject as 'the divine prophets' of 8:2; Hilgenfeld, as Lightfoot reports him, read it of the prophets after Moses.

title: The new yeast
sum: Let us not be blind to God's kindness: if he treated us as we treat him, we would be finished. As his disciples, let us live 'by Christianity'; whoever bears another name is not God's (10:1). Put away the old, sour yeast and change to the new yeast, which is Jesus Christ; be salted in him so as not to go bad (10:2). 'It is out of place to talk of Jesus Christ and live in the Jewish way. For Christianity did not put its faith in Judaism. Judaism put its faith in Christianity', in which every tongue that believed was gathered (10:3).

views.H: Lightfoot: this letter has the earliest known uses of the word 'Christianity' (10:1, 3). How scholars identify the 'Judaism' Ignatius opposes is the views note at 10:3.
views.N: 1 Corinthians 5:7-8 (old and new yeast), Galatians 2:14 ('live in the Jewish way'), Matthew 5:13 and Mark 9:50 (salt), Isaiah 66:18 (every tongue).
views.C: Whether and how the church and Israel are related is the card at Galatians 6. The site does not take Ignatius's contrast as a judgment on the Jewish people (topic Christian Anti-Judaism and the Bible).

echoes: 1 Corinthians 5:7-8; Galatians 2:14; Galatians 1:13-14; Matthew 5:13; Mark 9:50; Leviticus 2:13; Isaiah 66:18; Acts 11:26

settings.why: To give the warning its sharpest form: Christ is the new yeast, and to mix the old way with him is out of place. Knowing that he is writing to Christians, about a practice among Christians, keeps the words from being read as a statement about Jews.
settings.readers: A church that would have known Paul's letters on yeast and on living 'in the Jewish way' (1 Corinthians 5; Galatians 2) heard their words turned on a new question.

title: Truly and surely
sum: Ignatius does not write because he knows any of them hold the teaching, but to guard them in advance from 'the hooks of empty conceit'. Let them be fully convinced of the birth, the suffering and the resurrection, which happened 'in the time when Pontius Pilate was governor', done 'truly and surely by Jesus Christ, our hope' (11:1).

views.H: Naming Pilate fixes the events in time, as later in the creeds. Lightfoot reads the stress on 'truly' as aimed at the same teachers as chapters 8-10.
views.N: 1 Timothy 6:13 ('his good confession in front of Pontius Pilate'); 1 John 4:2 (Christ 'come in the flesh').

echoes: 1 Timothy 6:13; Luke 3:1; 1 John 4:2-3; Ignatius to the Trallians 9:1-2; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 1:1-2

settings.what: A confession of the true Christ
settings.to: The Magnesians, cleared of the teaching but warned
settings.when: At the end of the warning against false teaching
settings.why: To give them the facts to hold onto: birth, suffering, resurrection, under Pilate, done truly.
settings.readers: The Magnesians heard their own innocence stated ('not because I know that any of you are like this'), so the warning came as care, not accusation.

title: The modest Magnesians
sum: 'May I have the benefit of you in every way.' Though in chains, Ignatius is not equal to any of them who are free. They are not puffed up, for they have Christ within, and when praised they feel ashamed, 'as it is written, "A righteous person is his own accuser"' (12:1).

views.N: The quotation is of the Greek Proverbs 18:17, which differs from the Hebrew (see the note); 'puffed up' is Paul's word in 1 Corinthians 4:6 and 13:4.

settings.when: As the letter turns toward its close
settings.why: To praise without puffing up: he praises their modesty, and tells them that their blushing is itself righteous.
settings.readers: Hearers who had just been warned at length heard themselves praised, as Paul often closes with thanks.

title: Stand firm together
sum: Let them stand firm in 'the decrees of the Lord and of the apostles', so that all they do may turn out well, in flesh and spirit, faith and love, in the Son, the Father and the Spirit, with their overseer, their elders, 'that well-woven spiritual crown', and their deacons (13:1). Let them be subject to the overseer and to one another, as Christ to the Father and the apostles to Christ and the Father, so that there may be union of flesh and spirit (13:2).

views.N: Psalm 1:3 (in Lake's margin and his English), Acts 16:4 ('decrees'), Matthew 28:19 and 2 Corinthians 13:14 (Father, Son and Spirit), Ephesians 5:21 and 1 Corinthians 15:28 (being subject).
views.C: How the apostles' teaching and the church's tradition relate is the card at 2 Thessalonians 2:15.

echoes: Psalm 1:3; Acts 16:4; Matthew 28:19; 2 Corinthians 13:14; Ephesians 5:21; 1 Corinthians 15:28

settings.to: The Magnesian church and its leaders
settings.why: To sum up the letter: firmness in the apostles' teaching and union with the leaders, rooted in the union of Father, Son and Spirit.
settings.readers: The overseer, elders and deacons heard themselves named a last time with honor, and the church heard where its unity comes from.

title: Pray for Syria
sum: Knowing they are full of God, Ignatius has urged them briefly. He asks for their prayers, that he may reach God, and for the church in Syria, which he is not worthy to belong to, that it may be refreshed with dew through their church (14:1).

views.H: The church in Syria is Antioch, Ignatius's own; Lake's introduction counts help for Antioch among the aims of the letters. From Troas he later reports it at peace (Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 11:2).

echoes: Hosea 14:5; Psalm 133:3; Ignatius to the Romans 9:1; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 11:1-2

settings.when: Near the end of the letter
settings.why: To bind the Magnesians to Antioch by prayer, and to ask for his own perseverance to death.
settings.readers: A church that had sent four of its leaders to a prisoner was now asked to keep praying for his own church in Syria.

title: Greetings from Smyrna
sum: The Ephesians greet them from Smyrna, from where he writes; they have refreshed him, with Polycarp, overseer of Smyrna (the long recension reads 'you refreshed me'). The other churches greet them too. 'Farewell in God's harmony. Hold on to an unwavering spirit, which is Jesus Christ' (15:1).

views.H: The verse gives the place of writing, Smyrna, and names Polycarp as overseer there. Eusebius 3.36.5 gives the same setting.

echoes: Ignatius to the Ephesians 21:1; Polycarp to the Philippians 13:2; Ignatius to the Trallians 12:1

settings.when: At Smyrna, with the Ephesian delegates and Polycarp present
settings.why: To join the Magnesians to the other churches that were caring for Ignatius, and to end on the letter's theme, harmony.
settings.readers: Readers whose neighbors the Ephesians, within four hours' walk (Lightfoot), were with Ignatius when he wrote.
